card.hook: The E&O is so long and so white that it looks like a wedding cake someone stretched out along the seafront. Your only job is to get all of it in.
card.stand_here: Stand on Lebuh Farquhar, opposite the Heritage Wing, and face the building. The hotel is to the north of you, with the sea behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural, straight-on view. If you're close and the hotel won't fit, switch to 0.5x. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for windows and rooflines.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the façade up with the horizontal lines so the rooflines stay straight, then tap the white wall and slide it a touch darker so it keeps its detail against the sky.
card.best_time: Early morning is lovely, when the light from the sea falls flat across the white façade. For the grand front entrance, come back around sunset.
card.selfie_here: Head onto the seafront lawn and pose beside one of the old cannons, with the hotel behind you. For something a bit different, stand by the Java Tree on the lawn between the Heritage Wing and the Victory Annexe. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x so the long building fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the seafront lawn, facing the white façade, and ask them to step back so the whole wide building fits in with you.
card.rules_and_safety: Check on the ground whether the hotel's frontage and entrance area are open to the public. Watch for passing traffic and people on the street, and wait for a gap before you shoot. The Victory Annexe infinity pool isn't a public photo spot.
card.challenge: Get the façade perfectly level and symmetrical, with the main entrance dead centre and a little street at the bottom. Bonus points if no cars sneak in.
card.good_to_know: The Sarkies Brothers, who also founded Raffles in Singapore, opened the Eastern Hotel in 1884 and the Oriental Hotel the next year. They merged in 1889, and the present complex was finished in 1929. The hotel closed in 1996 for major rebuilding and reopened in 2001, and the 132-room Victory Annex tower was added in 2013.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Lebuh Farquhar, opposite the Heritage Wing, and face the building. The hotel is to the north of you, with the sea behind it.

card.hook: You'll spot this one before you've even checked the map: a huge house with deep indigo walls on Leith Street, standing out like a blueberry in a bowl of rice. It's the Cheong Fatt Tze Mansion, better known as the Blue Mansion.
card.stand_here: Stand on Lebuh Leith (Leith Street), on the pavement on the opposite side of the street from the mansion. Face the indigo facade straight on, and watch for traffic as you back up for the shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if the pavement is tight and you want the whole facade in one go. Zoom 1x looks more natural and less stretched. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the windows and trim.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the blue wall, then slide the brightness down a touch so the indigo stays rich instead of washing out.
card.best_time: Go before 10am or in the late afternoon, when the light is soft and the blue looks richest. One guide says strong afternoon sun washes the colour out.
card.selfie_here: Try the forecourt just before the main gate, where the whole indigo building fills the background. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the mansion rise up over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the street from the front of the mansion while you stand in front of it, or have them step back to the Stewart Lane junction for a wider shot with more sky.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed throughout the guided tour, but private hotel guest areas are off-limits. Sources disagree about photos inside, so check with staff when you arrive. One guide says selfie sticks aren't allowed, so leave yours in your bag.
card.challenge: Line the wall up with your gridlines so the house stands perfectly straight, then wait for a gap with no cars or people. Bonus points for patience!
card.good_to_know: Merchant Cheong Fatt Tze built the mansion at the end of the 19th century as his home and business base in Penang. The blue comes from lime mixed with natural indigo dye, which also helped keep the house cool. Local people bought it in 1989 to save it from development, and it has appeared in Indochine and Crazy Rich Asians.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Lebuh Leith (Leith Street), on the pavement on the opposite side of the street from the mansion. Face the indigo facade straight on, and watch for traffic as you back up for the shot.

card.hook: Church Street has plenty of handsome old buildings, but one of them is painted bright green and doesn't care who knows it. That's the Pinang Peranakan Mansion, and it's the easiest front in George Town to spot.
card.stand_here: Head for Pinang Peranakan Mansion on Church Street, where the phone icon sits right at the building. For the classic view, step back across Church Street where it's safe and turn around to face the green front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole front in. If the street is too narrow to step back, switch to zoom 0.5x, then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the doors and carved woodwork.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the green wall, then slide it a touch darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime, when the green really shows its colour. Early morning is usually quieter on the street, so you can wait for a gap in the traffic and people.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement in front of the main entrance with the emerald front behind you, and use the front camera. Hold your phone a little low and tilt it up so the mansion fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: No flash is allowed inside. Commercial photography needs permission from management. Guides disagree on whether you can photograph indoors, so check when you arrive. Watch for passing traffic on Church Street.
card.challenge: Take a straight-on shot of the green front, then sneak in a close-up of one doorway or carved detail, and see if a friend can guess which part of the mansion it is.
card.good_to_know: Chung Keng Quee, a wealthy 19th-century Chinese tycoon, bought the land in 1893 and had this mansion built in the 1890s as his home and office. It's Straits Eclectic in style, mixing European and Chinese ideas, with a five foot way along the side. It was originally white and was repainted green when it became a museum in the 1990s. A temple honouring Chung stands next door.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Pinang Peranakan Mansion on Church Street, where the phone icon sits right at the building. For the classic view, step back across Church Street where it's safe and turn around to face the green front.

card.hook: Picture a wooden walkway running out over the sea, with stilt houses squeezed in on both sides and a city skyline waiting at the far end. That's the Clan Jetties, and the planks do half the work for you.
card.stand_here: Walk out along the boardwalk on Chew Jetty to the seaward end, then turn round. Face back toward George Town so the row of stilt houses and the boardwalk lead your eye to the skyline.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the boardwalk and the houses. Go to 0.5x when you want the walkway to race away from you in one long line. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for roof edges, shrines and the skyline in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep the boardwalk in the middle, and hold the phone level so the house fronts stay straight.
card.best_time: Arrive about 30 minutes before sunset for the warm light. Early morning, before about 9am, also works well, with possible mist and fewer people.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x, with the boardwalk and houses stretching out behind you. Hold the phone a little low and out to the side, so the skyline fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: People live here, so this isn't a stage set. Keep to the main walkway, don't point your phone into open doors or windows, and ask before photographing anyone. Some side branches are private.
card.challenge: Find a shrine or another small detail of daily life, and frame it respectfully at 2x without a single doorway in the shot.
card.good_to_know: The jetties began after land was reclaimed along the old shoreline in 1882, which made landing jetties possible. Each one was settled by families from a particular Chinese clan, and the community grew slowly between the 1880s and the 1960s. Seven remain today: Ong, Lim, Chew, Tan, Lee, Mixed Clan and Yeoh.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk out along the boardwalk on Chew Jetty to the seaward end, then turn round. Face back toward George Town so the row of stilt houses and the boardwalk lead your eye to the skyline.

card.hook: A star-shaped brick fort sits right beside the sea, with a skinny steel lighthouse poking up at one corner. That's a lot of picture for one phone frame, and it's an easy one to get.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Esplanade, on the waterfront side, and face the fort's main entrance gate. The sea sits in front of you and the walls fill the middle of the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the gate and walls with the sea in front. Try zoom 0.5x if you want more sea and sky, or zoom 2x to home in on the gate.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the sea in the lower part of the frame and keep the horizon level, with the gate roughly in the middle and a little breathing space around it.
card.best_time: Late afternoon gives golden light on the sea. Morning is easier for the fort walls when you shoot from the Esplanade side.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Seri Rambai cannon in the northeast bastion, use the front camera and keep the fort walls behind you. Visit Penang says late-afternoon light comes into that bastion from the sea side, so it's kind to faces. If the moat walkway on the south and west sides is open, it's a good backdrop too.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the waterfront Esplanade, pointing their phone at the main entrance gate with the sea in front, while you pose between them and the fort.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed throughout the fort, including the museum and chapel-gallery, but no flash is allowed at the museum display cases. Parts of the fort were closed for restoration, so check current access, stay on the paths and don't touch the old structures.
card.challenge: Get the gate, the sea and a perfectly level horizon in one shot, then see if a passer-by can do it better than you.
card.good_to_know: Fort Cornwallis is the largest standing fort in Malaysia. The British East India Company finished it in 1810, on the site of a wooden stockade Captain Francis Light put up in 1786. The old moat was filled in during 1921 and has now been dug out again in the 2026 restoration. Inside, the Seri Rambai cannon was cast in 1603 and has travelled a long way since.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Esplanade, on the waterfront side, and face the fort's main entrance gate. The sea sits in front of you and the walls fill the middle of the frame.

card.hook: Picture shopfronts spilling sarees, garlands and spices right onto the pavement, with a bright temple gate in the middle of it all. That's Little India, and it's one of the most colourful corners of George Town.
card.stand_here: Walk to the Sri Mahamariamman Temple gate. You'll be about 75 m south of the district's marked centre, roughly a minute's walk, with the district lying to the north. Face the gate so the street scene wraps around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the gate and the street around it. If the street is too narrow to fit the whole gate in, tap 0.5x. Save zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for garlands, carvings and fabric displays.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the gate centred and the vertical lines straight, then tap the gate and slide the brightness down a little so the bright colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go around dusk, 6-7pm, when the lamps are lit and the archway and entrance glow. For a quieter scene, one guide suggests arriving before 6am, when devotees gather. Expect big crowds around Thaipusam and Deepavali.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the bright yellow arch on Market Street (Lebuh Pasar), where the street begins, so the arch is behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit it all in, and let the arch rise over your shoulder. It's 12.72 m tall and lights up at night, so it works after dark too. The Sri Mahamariamman Temple archway at dusk, when the oil lamps are lit, is another glowing backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: The streets are open to the public, but the temple is a place of worship. Photos are generally fine in the outer areas, but please ask before shooting inside.
card.challenge: Find one saree or garland in a colour that matches the gate, and get both in the same shot.
card.good_to_know: Little India is the Indian quarter in the middle of George Town. The Sri Mahamariamman Temple here is the oldest Hindu temple in Penang. Many of the Indian fashion shops are on Market Street, and street names can differ between maps and signs, so check the map.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the Sri Mahamariamman Temple gate. You'll be about 75 m south of the district's marked centre, roughly a minute's walk, with the district lying to the north. Face the gate so the street scene wraps around it.

card.hook: Your first photo here might be a car called Sally Carrera. She's an up-cycled star parked at the gate of an old bus garage, and she's perfect in the foreground.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, inside the Hin Bus Depot compound on Jalan Gurdwara. Face across the open lawn toward the mural walls and old brick buildings.
card.zoom: Use 1x for most shots of the lawn and murals. Switch to 0.5x for the entrance frame, or to fit a whole mural wall in when you're standing close.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the mural walls straight, then tap the mural so its colours look rich.
card.best_time: Sunday is the liveliest, because the market runs with around 70 stalls and the lawn is buzzing. It also means more people in your frame, so pick another day if you want it calmer, but check what's open first.
card.selfie_here: Try the open-air lawn inside the depot compound, where brick walls, market stalls and art backdrops surround you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold your phone a little low so the colourful wall fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an arts compound with events and a market, so check opening hours locally before you go. Photography signs may apply.
card.challenge: Get Sally Carrera in the foreground with the art deco entrance frame behind her, and see if you can make her look like she's about to drive off.
card.good_to_know: The depot was built in 1947 by Hin Company Ltd. to house its Blue Buses. It stood on what was then Brick Kiln Road, now Jalan Gurdwara. It closed in 1999, and was later refurbished to host the first art exhibition by Penang-based artist Ernest Zacharevic. The murals are by him and others, and they can be repainted, so what you see may differ a little from older pictures.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, inside the Hin Bus Depot compound on Jalan Gurdwara. Face across the open lawn toward the mural walls and old brick buildings.

card.hook: Komtar doesn't blend in, and that's why you'll love photographing it. This plain 1970s tower looms over George Town's old low-rise streets like it's lost its tour group.
card.stand_here: Stand on Jalan Penang, on the stretch in front of Komtar on the Penang Road side. Face the tower so it rises up over the street and the blocks around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole tower fits from bottom to top, and tilt your phone back as little as you can. Step back and try 1x for less stretching at the edges, or go to 2x-5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for a close-up of the top.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky stays blue and the tower keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Pick a bright, clear day. Traffic and people come and go, so take a few shots in a row and keep the one with the cleanest street. If Jalan Penang is too busy, Ria Road gives you a quieter angle across the low-rise buildings.
card.selfie_here: The best selfie spot is up on the Rainbow Skywalk, the glass-floored walkway on the roof of Komtar Tower (Level 68, The TOP). Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x and hold it out wide. Komtar won't be behind you though, because the city spreads out below you instead.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed at The TOP, but skip the flash in places like the aquarium to protect the animals. The glass floors can feel scary if you don't like heights, so wear comfy shoes. The street out front is a public road with traffic, so keep an eye out while you frame your shot. For the tower's ticketed areas, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the tower lined up with a vertical gridline, a strip of street at the bottom, and no one wandering through the middle. Bonus points if you manage it in under three tries.
card.good_to_know: Komtar's full name is the Tun Abdul Razak Complex, a group of five buildings, and Komtar Tower is the tallest. The complex opened on 2 December 1976 and Lim Chong Keat designed it as a "city within a city" on a 27-acre superblock. When it was finished in 1985 it was 231.7 metres, the tallest skyscraper in Southeast Asia, and renovations in 2015 took it to 248.7 metres. It's still a major bus terminal and the seat of Penang's state government.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Jalan Penang, on the stretch in front of Komtar on the Penang Road side. Face the tower so it rises up over the street and the blocks around it.

card.hook: Legend has it lightning burnt the first Khoo Kongsi down in 1901 because it looked too much like an emperor's palace. Stand in front of what replaced it and you'll see it's still pretty grand.
card.stand_here: Stand in the courtyard of Khoo Kongsi on Cannon Square, right where the phone icon sits, and face the front of the main hall. For a second angle, go to the entrance and point your phone up at the roof ridge.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front of the hall and its roof in one shot. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the carvings and gilded beams.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sky or roof and slide it a little darker so the roof detail doesn't wash out. If the carvings look dim, tap them and slide it brighter.
card.best_time: Aim for 9 to 10am. One walking guide says the sun lights the front of the hall then, and it's usually calmer and less crowded.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the front courtyard with the main hall behind you and use the front camera, or go to the top of the grand staircase beside the green stone lions with the temple behind you. Hold your phone a little low and a little back so the roofline fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand mid-distance in the middle of Cannon Square, facing the Leong San Tong prayer pavilion head-on, so the full roofline fits in the frame. You pose in front of the pavilion.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an active place of worship, so cover your shoulders and knees and respect worshippers and any signs. Flash may be restricted in some areas, so check signs first, and drones are generally not allowed. There's an entry ticket, so check the official site for opening times and ticket details.
card.challenge: Get the whole hall in one shot with a sliver of sky above the roof, then zoom in and find the most golden beam you can.
card.good_to_know: The Khoo clan first built a clanhouse here in 1851. The smaller version you see now was built from 1902 and finished in 1906. Chinese operas are still staged at the theatre during the seventh lunar month.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the courtyard of Khoo Kongsi on Cannon Square, right where the phone icon sits, and face the front of the main hall. For a second angle, go to the entrance and point your phone up at the roof ridge.

card.hook: Here's the trick on this street: the white domes and tall minaret rise right above the shophouse roofs, so one photo shows the mosque and the town around it. Not bad for one tap.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Lebuh Buckingham and Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling, on the pavement opposite the mosque's main facade. The mosque is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot, so face north-west and you'll see the front with its domes and minaret.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x from across the street to fit the facade, domes and minaret in one go. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the top of the minaret and the domes.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the minaret up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, and keep a strip of shophouse roofline in the frame to show the street scale.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, just before sunset, when the light on the white facade turns warm. Take your wide shot first, then walk closer for details.
card.selfie_here: Try the corner archway where Buckingham Street meets Pitt Street: stand under it with the minaret framed behind you, using the front camera (and 0.5x if your phone has it on the front). Its exact spot is a bit vague, so if you can't find it, the Pitt Street gate at the front also puts the minaret behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling (Pitt Street) from the front entrance, facing the Pitt Street gate so the whole mosque fits, while you pose at the gate.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship. Keep your photos to the outside and the courtyard, be discreet around people at prayer, and note that the worship hall is out of bounds to non-Muslims. If you're not dressed modestly, you can borrow a cloak at the entrance for free.
card.challenge: Get the minaret perfectly straight on a gridline with a slice of shophouse roof underneath, then see if your friends can guess which street you're on.
card.good_to_know: This was the first permanent Muslim institution in its area of George Town, built in the 19th century by Indian Muslim traders. The land goes back to 1801, when Sir George Leith appointed Cauder Mohudeen as head of the local South Indian Muslim community and granted him a plot. The look you see today comes from a 1930 renovation that enlarged the mosque and doubled the height of the central prayer hall.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Lebuh Buckingham and Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling, on the pavement opposite the mosque's main facade. The mosque is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot, so face north-west and you'll see the front with its domes and minaret.

card.hook: Don't come here for a grand palace, because this is a slim shophouse squeezed in among its neighbours on Armenian Street. The story is the star: a revolution got planned behind that front door.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement directly in front of No. 120 Armenian Street (Lebuh Armenian), right where the phone icon sits on the map, outside the Sun Yat-sen Museum Penang. Face the narrow shophouse front, which the street frames for you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a straight-on shot of the front. If the street is too tight to fit it all in, drop to 0.5x. Try 2x or more (depends on your phone) to pick out the door and the upper front.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the building up with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean, then tap the façade and slide it a little darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is soft and warm. Early morning also means fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the main entrance of the museum at 120 Armenian Street, under the Chinese arch, with the door and façade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the arch over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far side of Armenian Street, opposite the museum, while you stand by the front door, so the whole shophouse fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum inside is paid and ticketed, so keep to exterior shots unless you've checked the visitor photo rules. If you're bringing professional gear, ask the museum about its policy first.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice, once upright to catch the full height of the narrow house and once sideways to catch the street. Then pick the winner.
card.good_to_know: The house was built around 1880 as a townhouse and runs back about 40 metres from the street. In 1910 Sun Yat-sen brought his family to Penang and used it for meetings, including an emergency meeting to raise funds for an uprising in Guangzhou. The first issue of the Chinese newspaper Kwong Wah Yit Poh was published from this address in December 1910.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement directly in front of No. 120 Armenian Street (Lebuh Armenian), right where the phone icon sits on the map, outside the Sun Yat-sen Museum Penang. Face the narrow shophouse front, which the street frames for you.

card.hook: Picture red lanterns, curling incense smoke and dragons perched along the roof ridges, all in one frame. That's the Goddess of Mercy Temple, and it makes a great start to your George Town photo walk.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Lebuh Armenian and Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling, at the eastern end of Lebuh Armenian. Walk north-east towards the temple and face it, so the front courtyard, the roof and the lanterns are all ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole frontage in. If the forecourt and roof won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the roof ridges, dragon details and lanterns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the roof ridge up with a horizontal line, so the temple stands straight and doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Check the light on the day. Early in the day is often calmer, which gives you a clearer view of the frontage.
card.selfie_here: Try the front courtyard, facing Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling. Stand in the open square and face the street, so the temple facade is behind you. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) to catch the big bronze urns, giant joss sticks and curved roof ornaments over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the open front square across from the facade, so the whole temple fits in the frame, with you in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working temple, so be respectful. Photography is allowed inside, but without flash. Don't stand directly in front of people who are praying, and ask before taking close-ups of worshippers.
card.challenge: Count the dragons along the roof ridges, then zoom in to 5x (if your phone has it) and get a close-up of your favourite.
card.good_to_know: The Goddess of Mercy Temple, also called Kong Hock Keong, was built in 1800 and is described as the oldest Chinese temple in Penang. It began as a place to honour Mazu, a sea goddess for seafarers, and by 1824 it had become a Guan Yin temple. It was last renovated between 2012 and 2017.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Lebuh Armenian and Jalan Masjid Kapitan Keling, at the eastern end of Lebuh Armenian. Walk north-east towards the temple and face it, so the front courtyard, the roof and the lanterns are all ahead of you.

card.hook: A bright white church with a row of tall columns, sitting calmly in the middle of busy George Town. It's so neat and symmetrical that it almost looks like a stage set.
card.stand_here: Stand on Lebuh Farquhar, across the road from St George's Church, with the church to the west. Face it so the whole front and portico fit in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from across the road to catch the whole front. If traffic or parked vehicles push you close to the building, switch to 0.5x. Use 2x to pick out the steeple, and keep your phone level so the columns don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines, then tap the white front and slide it a little darker so the walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Skip Sundays, because they're for worship and the church is best photographed from the street then. Any other day, wait for a gap in the traffic and people before you tap the shutter.
card.selfie_here: Try the Francis Light Memorial on the church lawn, beside the domed memorial near the entrance. Use the front camera at 0.5x and put the church behind your shoulder. It's worth checking the exact spot when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the road on Lebuh Farquhar, facing the church so the whole building is in frame, while you stand in front of the church.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working church, so keep quiet and out of the way, and don't go in during services. Ask before photographing people. Wedding photography isn't allowed in the church area without permission. Opening hours vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get all the columns perfectly straight against the gridlines, with a little heritage shopfront peeking in at the edge.
card.good_to_know: St George's was finished in 1818 and consecrated in 1819. It's described as the oldest purpose-built Anglican church in Southeast Asia, and in 2007 it was named one of Malaysia's 50 National Treasures. The gabled roof replaced the original flat one in 1864, and the little domed pavilion in the grounds, from 1886, remembers Captain Francis Light.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Lebuh Farquhar, across the road from St George's Church, with the church to the west. Face it so the whole front and portico fit in your frame.

card.hook: Stand on Lebuh Queen and look up. The front of this temple is a crowd of painted gods and goddesses, and every one of them seems to be watching the street.
card.stand_here: Stand on Lebuh Queen, across from the front entrance, and face back toward the gopuram. If you can, back across the street so the whole painted gateway fits in with the street around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole gateway in. If people or parked vehicles force you to stand close, switch to zoom 0.5x, then use zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the sculpted figures above the entrance arch.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the facade, then slide it a touch darker so the colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer on all those colours. The temple may close for a break around midday, so check the opening hours before you go.
card.selfie_here: Head to the pedestrianised stretch of Lebuh Queen (Queen Street), a short walk down from the temple's main entrance. Use your front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the gopuram tower in view over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Lebuh Queen, on the street opposite the Queen Street entrance, so the whole gopuram tower and facade fit in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is an active place of worship. Photography inside isn't allowed, so keep your shots to the outside. Shoes come off before you go in, and shoulders and knees must be covered. Skip the flash and don't disturb worshippers, especially during prayers.
card.challenge: Pick your favourite sculpted figure on the facade, zoom in until it fills the screen, and see if a friend can spot which one you chose.
card.good_to_know: Sri Mahamariamman is the oldest Hindu temple in Penang. It's usually dated to 1833, though accounts vary on the exact year. Processions for festivals like Navarathiri and Chitraparuvam have set out from it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Lebuh Queen, across from the front entrance, and face back toward the gopuram. If you can, back across the street so the whole painted gateway fits in with the street around it.

card.hook: Picture a real bicycle bolted to a wall, with two painted kids riding it like they're about to pedal off down the street. You'll do a double take, and so will everyone around you.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement opposite the 'Children on a Bicycle' mural on Lebuh Armenian, close to the junction with Lebuh Cannon, and face the wall straight on. Check the exact wall on your map when you arrive.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the straight-on shot of the bicycle mural. Switch to 0.5x for a long view down the street with the shophouses on both sides, or try 2x or more (depends on your phone) to zoom in on the painted faces and leave out passers-by.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the wall square to the frame so the shophouse lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Go early, around 7-9am, before the tour groups arrive. Late afternoon or sunset also works, but it's busiest from late morning to mid-afternoon and at weekends.
card.selfie_here: The bicycle mural is the classic backdrop, but the queue for photos there is the longest on the street. For a quieter frame, try the corner of Lorong Love beside the 'Kids on Swing' mural. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the mural over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The street is open to the public, but the museums along it may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take the same wall twice, once close up on the painted faces and once wide with the neighbouring shopfronts, then see which one your friends like better.
card.good_to_know: Armenian Street began as a Malay lane, and by 1808 it was named after the Armenian traders who lived there. Chinese families later took over much of it and built clan houses nearby. In 1910 Sun Yat-sen chaired a conference in a townhouse here, which is now a museum. Murals can fade, so check what's currently on the wall.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement opposite the 'Children on a Bicycle' mural on Lebuh Armenian, close to the junction with Lebuh Cannon, and face the wall straight on. Check the exact wall on your map when you arrive.

card.hook: Don't worry if your photo of this tower looks a bit wonky. It really does lean a little, thanks to bomb damage in the Second World War. Your phone isn't to blame.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Lebuh Light and Lebuh Pantai, where Light Street meets Beach Street, right by the tower. The tower is just to the north-east, so face that way and you'll see the clock face with the colonial street corner around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole tower and the street corner into one frame. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to get close to the clock face and the cupola.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with an upright line, then step back instead of tilting your phone up, so the tower stays as straight as it can.
card.best_time: Go in daylight so you can see the clock face and all the detail. Early in the day is likely to be quieter for traffic, but check how the light falls when you get there.
card.selfie_here: Try the Fort Cornwallis side of the King Edward's Place roundabout, with the tower sitting in the middle of it. Use the front camera at 0.5x and check the screen to make sure the tower is over your shoulder, as we couldn't confirm it sits right behind you from this side.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by at the Light Street and Beach Street corner and ask them to frame you with the tower in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower sits in a busy roundabout between wide avenues with no pedestrian crossing close by. Take your photos from the pavement at the corner and cross carefully.
card.challenge: Can you get the clock face, the belfry and the copper-roofed cupola all in one shot, with you grinning at the bottom?
card.good_to_know: The tower was built for Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee and paid for by the Chinese business leader Cheah Chen Eok. Building began in 1900 and it opened on 23 July 1902. It rises about 30 metres (97 feet), and each of the 60 feet up to the clock is said to stand for one year of the Queen's reign. You can only see it from outside, as the inside isn't open to visitors.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Lebuh Light and Lebuh Pantai, where Light Street meets Beach Street, right by the tower. The tower is just to the north-east, so face that way and you'll see the clock face with the colonial street corner around it.

card.hook: Picture a three-tiered minaret poking up over old shophouse roofs, like it's peeking over a garden fence to see who's visiting. That's the scene at this corner of George Town.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Lebuh Acheh and Lebuh Cannon, where the mosque's street meets Cannon Street. Face the minaret rising above the corner; the mosque itself lies to the south-west. The spot is approximate, so shuffle a few steps if you need to.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the shophouses leading your eye up to the minaret, then switch to 1x for a calmer view of the street. Try zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out the minaret against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn the gridlines on, hold your phone upright and line the minaret up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and quieter streets. If you want to get closer to the entrance, skip prayer times.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the corner where Lebuh Cannon meets Lebuh Acheh, using the front camera with the minaret over your shoulder. Or step into the open grounds just inside the compound entrance gate, so the mosque stays in the frame behind you.
card.ask_someone: On Cannon Street, stand by the right-hand mural wall ('A Boy Reaching Up', if it's still there) and ask a passer-by to shoot back along the street, so the minaret shows at the far end behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship, so dress modestly near the entrance and keep a respectful distance from anyone praying. You can walk the grounds and take pictures, but non-Muslims can't enter the prayer hall.
card.challenge: Can you get the minaret so straight on a gridline that it would pass a school inspection, with one shophouse roofline in the frame for company?
card.good_to_know: The mosque was built in 1808 on land given by Tengku Syed Hussain Al-Aidid, an Acehnese aristocrat who had opened a Muslim settlement here in 1792. In the 19th century the area was sometimes called the Second Jeddah, because pilgrims gathered here before sailing to Mecca. The houses around the mosque are part of that original settlement, and the founder's family cemetery lies next to it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Lebuh Acheh and Lebuh Cannon, where the mosque's street meets Cannon Street. Face the minaret rising above the corner; the mosque itself lies to the south-west. The spot is approximate, so shuffle a few steps if you need to.
